title: Ad-Darr, who permits harm
hookLine: the one who permits harm as a test, always named beside An-Nafi' so that all is in His hand
tomorrow: Eli wants into a weekend art class. what can Amira actually give?

cards: The first sip of black coffee, before anyone gets used to it, is simply bitter. People who love it say the bitterness is part of the point. Yesterday's question: Dadi's knee aches in the damp.
What does she say to the ache? In Amira's house, it's short. Dadi winces, rubs the knee, and says: from Him, the ache, and from Him, the sabr, the patience.
Today's Name is one that needs care.

teach.b: Ad-Darr: the one who permits harm, as a test. Scholars who wrote on the Names, al-Ghazali among them, say it should never be said alone.

teach.h: HARM AND BENEFIT IN ONE HAND.
teach.b: It's named beside An-Nafi', the Benefactor, tomorrow's Name, so the two are heard together: harm and benefit, both in one hand. The Qur'an says it plainly.
If Allah touches you with harm, none can lift it but Him; and if He wants good for you, none can turn His bounty back. That isn't a God who enjoys pain.

teach.h: NOT RANDOM, NOT THE LAST WORD.
teach.b: It's a claim that nothing sits outside His hand, not even the ache, so the ache is neither random nor the last word. Then the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave the turn.

teach.h: GRATEFUL IN GOOD, PATIENT IN HARM.
teach.b: He said the affair of a believer is a wonder: if good comes, he is grateful, and that is good for him; if harm comes, he is patient, and that is good for him too.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in that hadith, even the bad day has a door into good, and the door is patience.
Patience isn't pretending. Dadi still winces. If you're carrying real pain right now, none of this says you deserved it.

how: When hardship comes, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to God and to Him we return, and ask for sabr, patience.

o: the one who permits harm, as a test
the Punisher, who hurts only sinners
the Destroyer of cities and nations

games.q: one hand, two Names — tap the pairs.

s: Ad-Darr means God enjoys causing harm
it's named beside An-Nafi': harm and benefit in one hand, harm permitted as a test.
scholars of the Names say Ad-Darr shouldn't be said on its own
al-Ghazali and others pair it with An-Nafi', the Benefactor.
in the hadith, patience in hardship becomes good for the believer
if harm comes, he is patient, and that is good for him.

games.q: you break your wrist right before the tryouts you trained for all year. a friend texts: 'everything happens for a reason, so be happy!' what's closer to today's lesson?
o: it hurts, it's in God's hand, and patience can turn it toward good.
be happy about it; pain is secretly good, so don't feel bad at all.
it's random bad luck; God isn't part of the hard parts of life.
games.why: the hadith doesn't ask for happiness about harm. it says patience in harm becomes good. the wince and the patience can sit together.

practice: If there's coffee, tea or a square of dark chocolate nearby, take one small bitter taste and let it sit on your tongue without reaching for water. Notice how the bitterness changes as you breathe.
With nothing to taste, sit with one small discomfort instead, a stiff shoulder or a cold room, and let it be there, patiently, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Ad-Darr. The one who permits harm as a test, never named alone, always beside An-Nafi', the Benefactor.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who permits harm, from the traditional list of the Names; said together with An-Nafi'.

carryVoice: Something to hold: all is in his hand, the bitter and the sweet, and the patience too. Day fifteen sixty-five.

sources.ref: Qur'an 10:107; 6:17 (harm none can lift but Him)
Sahih Muslim 2999 (the believer's affair is a wonder)
